Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.

papers.title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification
papers.abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.

papers.title: Ultrafast imaging of ring currents in atoms and condensed matter by electron scattering
papers.abstract: Ring currents are well known to generate magnetic fields. Despite the rich phenomena and detection of the ring current, an experimental reconstruction of the ring current at the atomic scale is still unsolved. In this work, we propose a method of resolving the ring current in a sample at the atomic scale by ultrafast electron diffraction. Inspired by the Rosenbluth formula, we study the electron diffraction of a sample with a ring current and separate the scattering cross sections into three kinds of response functions, which stand for the electric part, the magnetic part and the cross term, respectively. The ring current in the sample can be reconstructed from measuring the response function in different scattering configurations. Also, following the Rosenbluth formula, we propose that the response functions can be measured by fitting over fixed momentum transfer with different incident energy and relative direction, which is similar to the $ψ$-scan in crystal diffraction. With high-precision ultrafast electron diffraction, the magnetic part will be resolved despite being much weaker than the electric part. We simulate three examples with ring currents -- an ideal hydrogen atom, a circularly polarized helium atom ensemble, and a lithium crystal. Our model offers a promising way to resolve the current structure at the atomic scale.

papers.title: Predicting HCN, HCO$^{+}$, multi-transition CO, and dust emission of star-forming galaxies
papers.abstract: We present an analytical model of a turbulent clumpy star-forming disk that reproduces the spatially resolved observations for 6 molecular lines and 3 continuum bands at 250-700~GHz in the central 30~pc of the Circinus Galaxy. Using the properties of the stellar disk as input, and when matched to the line and continuum emission, the model yields the Toomre $Q$ parameter, mass accretion rate $\dot{M}$, metallicity $Z$, and cosmic ray ionization rate $ζ_{CR}$. These in turn are used to infer the gas properties (surface density, velocity dispersion, and radial velocity) as well as the star formation rate. Our main findings from the model include a low CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor that varies with radius in the range $α_{\rm CO}=0.5$--1.5 $M_{\odot}$pc$^{-2}/({\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1})$, close to the canonical value for such environments. It shows that CO(3-2) is a poor tracer of the gas mass surface density $Σ_{{\rm H}_2}$ on these small scales, which is better represented by molecules such as HCO$^+$(3-2) with higher critical density. The steep relation between $Σ_{{\rm H}_2}$ and star formation rate surface density $\dotΣ_*$ is typical of compact starburst systems, and the star formation rate (10~$M_{\odot}$kpc$^{-2}$yr$^{-1}$ averaged over the disk) is high enough to drive a wind. Despite this, and in contrast to typical large scale galactic disks, the energy injection rate into the ISM is dominated by gas inflow through the disk rather than the supernova rate. As such, the decreasing inflow rate at smaller radii could be caused by a wind, or indicate a recent increase of the mass inflow from larger scales. We suggest that such variations in the inflow rate could be associated with the nested spiral structures which have been observed in Circinus.

papers.title: Beyond Future Views: Exploring Future-State World Models for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

papers.title: Reset Quantum Channels
papers.abstract: We introduce Reset Quantum Channels (RQCs), a class of quantum channels acting on a Hilbert space structured as a direct sum of an arbitrary number of subspaces. Within each subspace, the state evolves unitarily; across subspaces, it is transferred by measure-and-prepare resets along given states. In this general setting, we show that the determination of their invariant states reduces to a stochastic eigenvalue problem, whose size is set by the number of reset states rather than by the dimension of the Hilbert space, and we discuss the uniqueness of these states. We further address the primitivity and the spectrum of these channels, which we compute explicitly when the reset states commute with the unitary evolutions. Applications include a small system coupled to several thermal reservoirs. We also consider random unitary evolutions and analyze the averages of the invariant states in this setup. Finally, we show that a suitable continuous-time limit yields Lindblad generators of reset type on the algebra of block-diagonal operators.

papers.title: Linear Quadratic Control With Event-Based Control Actions: Performance Beyond Periodic Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates linear quadratic (LQ) control for discrete-time stochastic systems to balance control performance and actuation rate. In our framework, the control input is sparse in time, and the actuation timings are determined in an event-based manner. We examine two types of problems: A sparsity-promoting regularization problem and a hard-constraint problem with a prescribed average actuation rate. Due to the combinatorial nature of these problems, finding optimal solutions is generally hard. Inspired by rollout algorithms in the context of dynamic programming, we develop a rollout-based approach to obtain tractable suboptimal policies. We show closed-loop stability and establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to classical periodic control. Moreover, under additional conditions, we quantify the performance improvement over periodic control and prove that this improvement is strictly positive. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in balancing control performance and actuation rate.

papers.title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
papers.abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.

papers.title: Claw-free difference graphs of finite groups
papers.abstract: Let $\D(G)$ be the difference graph of a finite group $G$: the graph on the non-isolated vertices of $\PE(G)-\Pg(G)$, where $x\sim_{\D} y$ if and only if $\gen{x,y}$ is cyclic and neither of $x,y$ lies in the cyclic group generated by the other. A claw is the graph $K_{1,3}$ and a graph is claw-free if it has no induced claw. We prove that for every finite group $G$, $\D(G)$ is claw-free if and only if it is a disjoint union of copies of the path $P_3$, if and only if the element orders of $G$ are prime powers or $6$, every element of order $3$ has at most one involution in its centralizer, and every involution has at most one subgroup of order $3$ in its centralizer (equivalently: $C_G(a)$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup of order at most $2$ for every $a$ of order $3$, and $C_G(u)$ a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup of order at most $3$ for every involution $u$). Consequences: a nilpotent group that is not a $p$-group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if $G\cong C_6$; $\D(\Sym_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 5$; $\D(\Alt_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 6$; a non-abelian simple group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if it is EPPO or $\PSL_2(11)$ or $\PSL_2(13)$, proved family by family (this uses the classification of finite simple groups). For soluble groups we obtain a complete classification: the non-EPPO soluble groups with claw-free $\D$ are $C_6$, $D_{12}$, $C_3\rtimes C_4$ and the Frobenius groups $N\rtimes K$ with $N$ an abelian $r$-group, $r\ge 5$, and $K\cong C_6$ or $C_3\rtimes C_4$. For every group with claw-free non-empty $\D$ we show $|O_2(G)|\le 2$ and $|O_3(G)|\le 3$, and we give non-soluble examples ($\Sym_5$, $\PGL_2(7)$, $\PSL_2(11)$, $\PSL_2(13)$). We also prove that the full enhanced power graph is claw-free only for cyclic groups and clarify the relations between claw-freeness of $\D(G)$, $\Pg(G)$ and $\PE(G)$.

papers.title: Explicit construction of the normal cone at every nonlocal extreme behaviour of $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$ and device-independent applications
papers.abstract: The set of quantum correlations $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$, in the simplest Bell scenario with two parties performing two binary measurements each, is an object of fundamental interest both in quantum foundations and for device-independent applications. A nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this set can maximize many different Bell expressions, yet these expressions are not all equally useful in a practical experiment. Here, firstly, we give an explicit characterization of every Bell expression maximized by any given nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this Bell scenario. This determines the full normal cone at every such behaviour and makes it possible to optimize over all Bell tests with the same ideal behavior. We then derive an exact variational formula for the quantum bound of an arbitrary Bell expression in this scenario. As an example illustrating the construction, we derive the normal cone for a family of extremal quantum behaviours of importance in device-independent randomness certification, from Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150403, 2022. Finally, we explore the consequences of this characterization for device-independent randomness generation in practical experiments. Specifically, for any given detection efficiency $η\in [0.75,0.98]$, we construct Bell tests and two-qubit experiments that certify more single-round min-entropy from one Bell score than any CHSH score can certify with the same detector efficiency, even when the quantum devices used for the CHSH test are optimized. The results provide a systematic way to choose Bell tests for a desired quantum behaviour and to improve their performance for device-independent applications under experimental imperfections.

papers.title: Projector Time Map Calibration for Event-based Structured Light
papers.abstract: Existing event-based structured light obtains a dense projector-camera correspondence from the timestamp of an event. It assumes that the projector scans a parallel raster and that the sensor timestamps each pixel independently, and we show that neither assumption holds. We obtain the correspondence from a temporal code that identifies the projector pixel directly and therefore needs no prior calibration, we calibrate the projector time map from the same recording, and we recover the geometry of the system and the offsets between its clocks by a spatio-temporal self-calibration in a preamble of a few seconds that needs no reference object and no second camera.

papers.title: Neural variational Skyrmions as a topological benchmark: emergent symmetry, precision energies and KAN--MLP comparison
papers.abstract: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time. We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.

papers.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
papers.abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

papers.title: Obliquity of Mercury with a fluid core and a deformable mantle
papers.abstract: In anticipation of BepiColombo's orbital insertion in 2026, this study revisits the rotation of Mercury, modelling it with a fluid core and a deformable mantle. For this well-established physical model, we provide an analytical solution based on a novel Lagrangian formalism. Our approach enables a comprehensive 3D solution for the mantle's orientation, including the phase in longitude at the perihelion. The model incorporates dissipative torques from core-mantle boundary friction and tidal deformations, conservative pressure torques, and the effect of the planet's apsidal precession. We validate the equilibrium positions obtained numerically in previous studies, but identify discrepancies in earlier analytical works. These inconsistencies overestimated the out-of-Cassini-plane offset induced by tidal deformation by a factor of 100. Additionally, we explore the parameter space to determine where the spin axis deviates most from the Cassini plane and identify a region exhibiting bifurcation in the spin axis equilibrium position. This region cannot be adequately analysed using a model linearised with respect to the obliquity angle.

papers.title: Structure-preserving compression of Matrix Product States
papers.abstract: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control the growth of bond dimensions, but compression can break the conservation laws of the equation being solved. A truncation is not the flow of a Hermitian generator, so even a small truncation error can violate exact algebraic identities of the Schrödinger equation. For any matrix product state integrator that leaves the state in canonical form with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant after compression whenever the resulting scalar quadratic constraint equation admits a real root, without enlarging any bond dimension. Rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers when that correction fails. The geometry of the low-rank manifold provides sufficient conditions for conservation by the fixed-rank projected flow and bounds what corrections within a frozen center frame can achieve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories.

papers.title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
papers.abstract: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.

papers.title: How many states does an exact relaxation model need? Sharp state complexity and geometric obstructions for reversible chains
papers.abstract: How many states does a reversible Markov model need to reproduce two prescribed relaxation modes exactly? We maximize the smaller of the two stationary coordinate variances over all finite reversible chains whose states lie in a given convex region and whose coordinates relax at rates $1$ and $ρ$. Detailed balance turns this into the equilibrium of a tension-only cable network whose loads depend on the stationary masses. For the moment curve of the Wright-Fisher diffusion no finite chain is optimal: maximizing sequences converge to a unique beta law, and the best deficit with $N$ states is of order $N^{-2}$. We find the exact leading constant for states on the curve and for states in its convex hull, together with the optimal cube-root density of states. The hull constant is the curve constant times $c/(1+c)$, $c=(ρ-2)/ρ$; at $ρ=5/2$ the hull needs $\sqrt{6}$ times fewer states, although the limiting law is the same. For $ρ>8/3$ any upward enlargement of the hull lowers the constant again. All lower bounds hold for arbitrary transition graphs. At every fixed number of states an optimizer exists. On a seven-gon the smallest optimal chain jumps from three to four states while the optimal value stays constant, and a family of polygons forces the state count to grow linearly with the number of sides. Monotone vector fields give exact upper certificates, which solve an asymmetric quadrilateral at all rates and 381 polygon-rate instances in exact arithmetic. We formulate a finite-realizability problem and a finite-dictionary conjecture for polygons, and derive state budgets and exclusion tests for finite kinetic models.

papers.title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
papers.abstract: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

papers.title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
papers.abstract: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of every word, and a statistical model that takes into account that the spread of difficulty between requests itself depends on the load restores, for each component, the laws of its dependence on every kind of load. These laws make up the passport of a model. The paper presents the method of the separation, the principles of constructing the laws and the passports of seven models built by this method; the separation opens the way to studying the fine structure of the behavior of a neural network.

papers.title: Improved perimeter bounds for Hausdorff approximation by convex polygons
papers.abstract: We investigate how closely a convex polygon with at most n vertices can approximate a plane convex body of given perimeter. For free approximation in the Euclidean Hausdorff metric we improve Popov's bound for every $n \geq 3$. We also improve his inscribed bound for every $n \geq 3$ and his circumscribed bound for $n = 3$. The common step is to join successive boundary contacts of the body and estimate the perimeter lost in passing to their convex hull.

papers.title: Quantum computing for gearing down complex many-fermion problems
papers.abstract: Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale {\it ab initio} calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex {\it ab initio} many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Decodability: Understanding and Improving Instruction Following in World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$Δ$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.

papers.title: Active Learning of Flows from Curve Observations using Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: The active learning of real control systems requires informative roll-outs of controls. In this paper, we present a local optimization algorithm that finds the trajectory that most reduces uncertainty about the flow of a control system modeled by a Gaussian process. Therefore, we derive an approximation scheme for the posterior kernel of the Gaussian process after observing it on an entire continuous-time trajectory and establish a Pontryagin-type necessary condition for the optimizer. As the flow is unknown, the actual trajectory can deviate from the planned trajectory. We propose a trajectory planner that searches for the most informative control within a maximal allowed deviation horizon instead of a fixed time horizon. We show by trajectory-wise time rescaling that the underlying optimal control problem is equivalent to a fixed end time optimal control problem. Finally, we study both the fixed end time planner and the fixed maximum deviation planner in a numerical example and compare them with benchmarks.

papers.title: Adaptive Redescending Regression with $q$-Polynomial Losses
papers.abstract: We introduce a family of smooth $q$-polynomial losses for robust joint regression--scale estimation. The family contains the Cauchy loss at $q=1$ and converges pointwise to the squared loss as $q$ increases. For every finite $q$, its regression score is bounded and redescending, while its scale score is bounded and permits explicit analysis of scale existence. We formulate simultaneous estimation through a surrogate likelihood with a common scale calibration $κ=1/2$ and select $q$ by maximizing the normalized surrogate likelihood over a finite candidate set. We investigate existence, large-sample behaviour, and the robustness implications of the loss family and discuss how optional modification of the scale score, for example by taking $κ=q/2$, can increase the threshold against scale explosion. This breakdown-oriented adjustment is distinct from the baseline estimator and requires its own joint breakdown analysis. An MM-type algorithm provides a practical implementation. Numerical investigations assess the resulting robustness--efficiency trade-off under different tail regimes.

papers.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking

papers.title: AnyBodyCodec: A Shared Native Interface for Body-Model Conversion, Extension, and Humanoid Control
papers.abstract: Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches 16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes take 7.43-7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget, aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate 160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together, these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream policy compatibility.

papers.title: ParaBMG: A Parallel Block Multigrid Framework for Large-Scale Evolving Sparse Systems on Unstructured Meshes
papers.abstract: Solving large-scale, evolving sparse linear systems on unstructured meshes remains the primary performance bottleneck in many GPU-accelerated geometry processing pipelines. Although modern linear solvers like multigrid and multilevel additive Schwarz (MAS) methods offer fast convergence and strong parallelization potential, a unified benchmark and solver design tailored for geometry processing tasks have been lacking. Addressing this gap, we present ParaBMG, a parallel block multigrid preconditioning framework that combines fully parallel geometric hierarchy construction, fast block-Jacobi smoothing, and GPU-optimized operators. We develop CUDA implementations of four standard geometry processing pipelines to form a large-scale benchmark for GPU linear solvers, comprising more than 40K linear systems with up to 6.6M unknowns. Across comparisons in this dataset, ParaBMG achieves speedups of 3.7x-7.7x over strong general-purpose algebraic multigrid baselines, 6x-105x speedups over our custom GPU implementations of the state-of-the-art CPU multigrid solvers for Poisson problems, and 6x-96x speedups over MAS. Compared with open-sourced multigrid baselines, ParaBMG reduces repeated hierarchy construction costs through hierarchy reuse and improves convergence through MAS-inspired block-Jacobi smoothing. Compared with MAS, the complementary coarse corrections reduce iteration counts by an order of magnitude while maintaining low per-iteration costs. It enables three interactive geometry processing applications with order-of-magnitude speedups over their public implementations.

papers.title: Real stable multivariate Delannoy polynomials and their Rayleigh differences
papers.abstract: The univariate Delannoy polynomials are known to have only real zeros. We construct a real stable multivariate refinement of these polynomials using weighted lattice paths and give both algebraic and combinatorial proofs of stability. More strongly, we show that every Rayleigh difference of the multivariate Delannoy polynomials is a perfect square and give an explicit factorization.

papers.title: Boundary concentration and Pohozaev identity for the fractional p-Laplacian
papers.abstract: We prove a Pohozaev-like identity for bounded weak solutions of the fractional p-Laplace equation with a locally Lipschitz nonlinearity on bounded C^2 domains, provided that s>max{1/2-1/p,0}. We compare the weak equations for the solution and its spatial deformation to show that the first-order contribution of the energy remainder is concentrated at the boundary. The boundary term involves the weighted trace, with a coefficient expressed by an integral of the one-dimensional boundary profile.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Model Reduction of Metriplectic Systems via Oblique Projections and Block Structure
papers.abstract: Metriplectic systems combine conservative and dissipative dynamics and are characterized by energy conservation and entropy production. The degeneracy conditions underlying these properties are generally not preserved by standard projection-based model order reduction. We develop two structure-preserving reduction strategies. The first enforces degeneracy conditions through oblique projections and combines gradient-preserving and matrix empirical interpolation for hyper-reduction. The second constructs reduced bases adapted to available operator block structure, preserving degeneracy without online oblique corrections. We establish sufficient conditions for preserving the Jacobi identity and derive a priori error estimates. Numerical tests on benchmark problems demonstrate accuracy, thermodynamic consistency, and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Hall effect in electrolyte solutions: Self-consistent Debye-Huckel-Onsager theory
papers.abstract: A self-consistent statistical-mechanical theory of the Hall effect in electrolyte solutions is developed by extending the self-consistent Debye-Huckel-Onsager (SCDHO) framework to crossed electric and magnetic fields. The theory incorporates non-local ionic charge distributions through Slater-type form factors and ion-specific coefficients describing the effective Lorentz response, with experimental input for protons and hydroxide ions. Within the random-phase approximation, the Hall conductivity is expressed as mean-field, correlation, and electrophoretic contributions. Both interaction channels include the Lorentz rotation of the complete electric-field-induced ionic velocity. In the point-charge limit with hydrodynamics suppressed, the relaxation correction agrees with independent odd stochastic density functional theory and the relaxation part of Friedman's classical result. For 22 dilute aqueous electrolytes, the mean absolute relative deviations from measured Hall constants and Hall numbers are about 17 percent. At finite concentrations, the theory predicts a nonmonotonic Hall number for NaBPh4 and sign changes of the electrophoretic correction for NaI and HCl. Correlation effects dominate for HCl and LiOH, whereas the two interaction channels become comparable for KOH and aqueous imidazolium salts. The results clarify how ionic mobilities, effective Hall coefficients, charge distributions, and solvent hydrodynamics determine electrolyte magnetotransport.

papers.title: Pure Orbitronics: Hall Responses and Torques by Orbital Exchange in Spinless Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides
papers.abstract: Recent studies have identified orbital exchange fields as a novel mechanism for controlling electronic and magnetic phenomena through the orbital degree of freedom. In contrast to conventional spin exchange fields, orbital exchange fields couple directly to orbital angular momentum and can emerge from purely orbital interactions or dynamically through couplings to chiral excitations such as phonons and magnons. Motivated by these developments, we investigate the transport and torque responses generated by orbital exchange fields in two-dimensional materials. Using monolayer H-phase MoS$_2$ as a prototypical transition-metal dichalcogenide, we introduce a Zeeman-like orbital exchange field that breaks time-reversal symmetry in orbital space while leaving the spin degree of freedom inactive. We demonstrate that this perturbation induces a sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity even in the absence of spin magnetism and spin--orbit coupling driven mechanisms. Simultaneously, the orbital Hall response remains robust in the weak-field regime and undergoes substantial reconstruction at larger exchange strengths due to pronounced band modifications. In addition, we show that currents can generate sizable current-induced orbital torques on the orbital magnetization. Our results establish orbital exchange fields as an effective route toward Hall transport and nonequilibrium torque phenomena driven purely by orbital physics, opening new perspectives for orbitronics and orbitally engineered quantum functionalities.

papers.title: Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents
papers.abstract: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line. Across 1,605 MIRA-v2, CDM, VivaBench, and in-hospital liver malignancy primary cohort cases, MIRA-v2 single-run top-50% pass rate reached 98.91%, matching five-run consistency, saving ~80% compute; CDM achieved 96.00% test attainment by escalating to the five-run consistency tier; cross-specialty, missing-imaging, and combined enriched cohorts entered the full-deferral tier, capping calibration false-certification rate at 0.00%-3.50%.

papers.title: Beyond What They Say: Cue Acknowledgment and Robustness in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Explanations are used to assess whether vision-language models rely on visual evidence or misleading suggestions. A response that explicitly names a cue can still follow it, making disclosure alone an incomplete basis for judging robustness. We ask whether greater cue acknowledgment accompanies greater resistance. We compare matched answers and explanations under helpful, misleading, and conflicting visual and textual cues while holding the underlying question and correct answer fixed. A paired comparison shows that a model can select the endorsed wrong answer more often while acknowledging the cues more often. Reduced silence therefore need not indicate improved resistance. Explanations may also mention a textual suggestion while omitting an accompanying visual cue. Requesting evidence and acknowledgment does not consistently improve resistance in the tested settings. Outcomes vary across models and settings, and these comparisons do not isolate a causal effect of acknowledgment. Evaluations should report cue following and acknowledgment on the same instances, distinguishing visual from textual cues.

papers.title: What Stays in the Picture? From Redundant Instructions to Dependency-Aware Image Editing
papers.abstract: We introduce complex redundant-instruction image editing, where a single request specifies multiple objects, their attributes, and spatial relations while revising or canceling earlier editing requirements. Direct editing can fail to recover this intent, while splitting the request into successive steps can preserve obsolete edits and visual errors. Our key insight is to resolve the revision history into a final editing target that jointly guides planning and verification, so that obsolete requests do not become visual edits. Based on this insight, CRIE-Agent learns to consolidate revisions into object-level final intent and executes the retained objects in reference-first blocks, establishing referenced objects before their dependents. Verification then guides complete re-execution from the source image, with conditional layout hints, preventing visual errors from failed attempts from being carried into subsequent ones. We also construct CRIE-S, a benchmark containing 10,000 complex and redundant editing instructions with exact final intent annotations. Across five image-editing backends on CRIE-S, CRIE-Agent raises complete editing success from 0% under direct editing to 27.5--50.0%.

papers.title: Finite Angular Derivative Sets and Almost Isometries of the Hyperbolic Disc
papers.abstract: We prove that a subset $E$ of the unit circle is the set of points at which an analytic self-map of the unit disc has a finite angular derivative if and only if $E$ is an $F_σ$ set. We also prove that, for every countable dense subset $E$ of the unit circle, there exists an almost isometry in the sense of Garnett--Papadimitrakis whose angular derivative is finite precisely on $E$.

papers.title: Pushy Random Walk on the Bethe lattice: a Galton-Watson perspective
papers.abstract: Pushy random walks are minimal models of transport in deformable media, in which the walker displaces the obstacles it bumps into rather than being blocked by them. On the Bethe lattice, we show that the walkable structure dynamically created by a pushy walker can be generated a priori as an explicit multi-type Galton-Watson tree, so that the walker reduces to a simple random walk on a static random tree, and its escape to infinity coincides with the survival of the underlying branching process. Standard generating-function tools then give direct access to the escape properties of these walks. For the Sokoban walk, which pushes a single obstacle, we recover the known critical density $ρ_c = 1-(z-1)^{-2}$ and the behavior of the escape probability close to $ρ_c$, and derive its small-density asymptotics. For the second-order pushy walk, which can push trains of two obstacles, we establish the conjectured $ρ_c = 1-(z-1)^{-3}$, and compute the escape probability at all densities. Beyond escape, the same framework yields the statistics of the trace of trapped walkers: the distribution of the maximal depth follows from the extinction probabilities, while the distributions of the visited volume and of the number of dead ends are encoded in explicit functional equations for their generating functions, which we invert numerically. All predictions agree with Monte Carlo simulations.

papers.title: Very weak solutions of nonlinear elliptic systems with Orlicz growth
papers.abstract:
In this work we consider non-linear elliptic equations with respect to Orlicz growth, for instance equations of the form $$ \mathrm{div}(φ(\vert 
abla u \vert) 
abla u)= 0. $$ We study very weak solutions to this system, that is, solutions that are not a priori in the correct energy space to this equation ($φ(\vert 
abla u \vert) \vert 
abla u \vert^2 \in L^1$). On the one hand, using rather mild assumptions on the corresponding Orlicz space (we need either the $Δ_2$ or $
abla_2$ condition, but not both at the same time), we can show that the integrability of very weak solutions improves to the energy space, provided that the initial integrability is close enough to the energy space. On the other hand, mirroring the construction of Colombo and Tione (Non-classical solutions of the $p$-Laplace equation, J. Eur. Math. Soc., 2024), for the $p$-Laplacian, we give a construction of 'wild' solutions for a $L \log L$-type Laplacian.

papers.title: Frustration-Stabilized Hexamerons and Their Topological Magnons in Janus MXene
papers.abstract: Frustrated magnets on triangular lattices favour noncollinear order, and when inversion symmetry is broken they can host localized topological textures on top of that order. Here we show that the Janus MXene MnHf2C2FI is such a system. Combining first-principles calculations with atomistic spin simulations, we find that magnetism is confined to the Mn layer, where a strong antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor exchange together with a sizable Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction stabilizes a frustrated 120 Neel ground state. On top of this ground state we identify a metastable hexameron: a composite of six merons and antimerons, one vortex-antivortex pair on each of the three sublattices, whose sublattice-resolved topological charges compensate. Linear spin-wave theory confirms that the hexameron is a local energy minimum, and its noncoplanar cores act as potential wells that bind discrete in-gap magnon modes below the bulk continuum. In a periodic hexameron array the magnon bands carry nonzero Chern numbers, and the resulting Berry curvature produces a magnon thermal Hall response whose sign depends on which of the two time-reversal partners of the hexameron is realized. Our results establish Janus MXenes as a two-dimensional platform in which frustration, broken inversion symmetry, and spin-orbit coupling combine to produce metastable antiferromagnetic solitons with distinct spectroscopic and transport fingerprints.

papers.title: PanoUAV-Track: Full-Spherical UAV Visual Tracking in the Wild
papers.abstract: Existing UAV tracking benchmarks predominantly rely on perspective cameras with limited fields of view. Omnidirectional cameras enable full-spherical observation, yet tracking from moving UAV platforms remains largely unexplored. Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras observe targets across both azimuth and elevation, introducing geometric challenges under equirectangular projection (ERP). To investigate this setting, we capture approximately \textbf{40 hours of real-world 8K panoramic UAV video} and construct \textbf{PanoUAV-Track} through temporal clip extraction, target annotation, and the integration of simulated sequences. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering real-world daytime and nighttime scenes alongside simulation, and supporting both visual and language-based target specification. Through extensive evaluations, we reveal a clear \textbf{perspective-to-spherical} generalization gap and identify tracking degradation associated with latitude-dependent distortion and ERP seam discontinuity. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. PUTrack improves zero-shot and in-domain tracking, particularly for seam-crossing targets. Code and benchmark resources will be available\footnote{\textcolor{tabpink}{https://libingyu01.github.io/PanoUAV-Track/}}.

papers.title: A Structured Levenberg--Marquardt Method for Binary Tensor Completion
papers.abstract: We develop a structured Levenberg--Marquardt (LM) method with trust-region globalization for binary tensor completion, using triple decomposition and a logistic loss. Under a local component-residual error bound and positive outer curvature, we prove quadratic convergence of the exact iteration for damping exponents $1\leδ\le2$, without requiring full row rank. A constant-rank criterion and an explicit rank-one certificate provide sufficient conditions for the residual error bound. The analysis decomposes the local error into outer-loss linearization, factor linearization, and regularization contributions. For a symmetric nonquadratic logistic--LSE family with $δ=2$, cancellation improves the objective-model error to fourth order and the decrease-ratio error to second order. A synthetic experiment illustrates the local quadratic convergence rate. On the HCP and Enron datasets, the proposed method improves binary tensor completion accuracy while requiring fewer outer iterations than the first-order methods.

papers.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

papers.title: A Combinatorial Construction of Symmetric Magic Squares of Order Four
papers.abstract: We construct all symmetric nonnegative integer matrices of order four having a common sum on every row, column, and both diagonals. The construction is a disjoint union of twelve translates of free submonoids, each with five uniquely determined nonnegative integer parameters.Twelve is the smallest possible number of classes among finite disjoint unions of translates of free submonoids generated by five elements, even when generators outside the Hilbert basis are allowed. A comparison-based case analysis supplies integer inverse formulas and assigns every point on the shared faces to exactly one class. The normal forms prove that the twelve primitive extreme-ray generators form the entire Hilbert basis: eight have magic sum two and four have magic sum four. We exhibit the underlying regular unimodular triangulation and a single perturbation direction producing all half-open boundary conventions. The resulting positive multivariate generating function specializes to an explicit rational function and a quasipolynomial of period four in the magic sum. A further consequence is a reflexive lattice polytope associated with positive symmetric magic squares.

papers.title: A Lightweight Method for Validating Simulated LiDAR Configurations Based on Point Density over Distance
papers.abstract: Simulated LiDAR sensors play a crucial role in validating autonomous systems, yet achieving signal-level realism remains challenging due to simplified sensor models and limited configurability in common simulation environments. This paper presents a lightweight, platform-agnostic method to assess one observable aspect of LiDAR simulation fidelity: the range-dependent point density on annotated objects. The method uses only 3D bounding boxes and point clouds and does not require semantic labels, detailed maps, simulator internals, or perception models. To quantify agreement between real and simulated range-dependent point distributions, we formulate the Density Similarity Score (DSS), a bounded similarity representation derived from the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) over discretized distance bins. The method is evaluated against a real-world LiDAR using three CARLA configurations of varying complexity. Results show that naive parameter matching based on sensor datasheets leads to systematic point-density deviations, particularly in the near field, while a custom configuration using the sensor's non-uniform vertical beam angles achieves the highest similarity in the evaluated scenario (DSS: 0.559--0.709). The proposed approach is intended as an early-stage, signal-level consistency check for identifying gross mismatches in simulated LiDAR configurations. It should be interpreted as a complementary validation step rather than a complete measure of simulation quality or downstream perception performance.

papers.title: Pairing and modular: Generalized electrons and quasiholes inside the $\boxtimes$ of topological orders
papers.abstract: We study the relationship between the pair creation mechanism in physics and the pairing ($\boxtimes_{\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}}$) in mathematics, focusing on the modular and algebraic properties. We provide a way to couple two topologically ordered systems, $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A'}$ sharing the common (non-group-like) structure $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}=\overline{\mathbf{A'}_{\text{ub}}}$, through the nonabelian anyon analog of the pair creation mechanism denoted as $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}=\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}\boxtimes \mathbf{A'}_{\text{ub}}$. We identify $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$ as the generalized version of electron operators in general topological orders or hidden current with (half-)integer spin involving the conformal embeddings. We provide a way to construct $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$ as the hidden topological operator and identify $\mathbf{A}\boxtimes_{\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}}\mathbf{A'}$, a general class of topoloical orders, as the $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$-extended symmetry topological field theory. We also conjecture a series of underlying (unexplored) modular invariants, connecting the conformal embedding and the pairing.

papers.title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.

papers.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
papers.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

papers.title: Gumbel Substitution: Removing Sampler Drift from RL Without Trusting the Sampler
papers.abstract: When RL rollouts come from untrusted samplers on arbitrary hardware, precision and checkpoint lag, the sampling distribution $q$ differs from the trainer's policy $p$, and training on the sampler's tokens adds a drift term equal to supervised fine-tuning toward $q$. Published corrections (TIS, MIS, IcePop, score centering, GSPO, CISPO) all need $q(y)$, which a permissionless sampler reports and can misreport. We introduce Gumbel substitution. The coordinator fixes public Gumbel noise for every token position, bit-identical across GPUs, and the sampler draws $y=\arg\max(\ell^q+G)$. The trainer recomputes $v^*=\arg\max(\ell^p+G)$, the token its own policy would have drawn with the same noise, and scores $v^*$ in the sampler's context. For a sampler that follows the protocol, $v^*$ is an exact sample from $p$ given the prefix, so the drift vanishes in expectation for any $q$, without sampler-reported probabilities. We measure the residual left by the deployed heads, bound the one added by admission gates, and state what an adaptive sampler can still do. The same comparison gives a per-token match rate that admits and pays samplers. In the lab, on a 9B model with the same head on both sides, the expected drift of uncorrected training is at least 170 to 4,800 times that of substitution. On a 2B model under strong mismatch, uncorrected training collapses while substitution stays stable, comparable to MIS with score centering given the true $q$. On a permissionless network, a 9B model was trained for 158 optimizer steps on 15.75B tokens from heterogeneous samplers, with no skipped step and 1.21% of tokens substituted; it improved on all eight held-out benchmarks.

papers.title: Efficient Analysis of Numerous Galactic Compact Binaries via the Free-bin Scheme
papers.abstract: Global analysis of Galactic compact binaries (GCBs) for space-based gravitational-wave detectors is computationally demanding in the high-frequency region (above $\sim$10 mHz), where resolvable signals are sparse but frequency samples are numerous. We propose a free-bin scheme that evaluates the nontrivial likelihood only in movable frequency windows centered on sampled signal frequencies. The method preserves the joint-likelihood structure by replacing only the signal-containing regions of a precomputed null likelihood, and avoids the fixed-bin edge effect by construction because the windows follow the sampled frequencies. In a simulated TianQin dataset containing 193 GCBs, 192 injected sources are recovered with waveform fitting factors above 0.99. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that the free-bin and conventional full-band likelihood implementations yield identical results when the same finite-length local waveforms and numerical settings are used. Computational benchmarks show that the acceleration is primarily controlled by the fraction of the frequency domain covered by the merged signal windows and decreases as this coverage increases.

papers.title: GeoSDF-Diff: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Planning for Collision-Free Trajectories
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently attracted increasing attention in motion planning due to their ability to model high-dimensional and multi-modal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion-based planners still struggle to reliably satisfy geometric feasibility in unseen cluttered environments with complex obstacle layouts. To address this challenge, we propose GeoSDF-Diff, a geometry-aware diffusion planner that incorporates multi-scale SDF conditioning into trajectory denoising. The key idea is to provide the denoiser with both route-level geometric context and fine local clearance evidence, enabling generated trajectories to better adapt to unseen complex obstacle layouts. Specifically, a Geometric Encoder extracts multi-scale SDF features and injects them into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention. We further introduce a trajectory-level training objective that combines SDF clearance, violation emphasis, smoothness, and path-length regularization, so that local infeasibilities are penalized during training rather than corrected only at inference time. Experiments on held-out cluttered environments show that, without post-hoc trajectory repair or sampling-time guidance, GeoSDF-Diff achieves a 65.2% average success rate across diverse test scenarios, outperforming strong diffusion baselines by 25.4% to 28.5%.

papers.title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

papers.title: Balanced Boolean Functions from Sparse Niho-Type Permutation Polynomials: Few-Valued Walsh Spectra and Applications
papers.abstract: We study balanced Boolean functions parameterized by two-to-one mappings of the forms $P(x+x^2)$ and $P(x+x^{-1})$, where $P$ is a sparse permutation polynomial with generalized Niho-type exponents. First, for $q=2^m$ with $m$ even, we determine the complete four-valued Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function parameterized by $Q(x+x^2)$, where $Q(x)=x(1+x^{q-1}+x^{2(q-1)})$. We then generalize a permutation polynomial studied by Gupta and Sharma to the parameterized family $P_λ(x)=x^{3q-1}+λx^{2q}+λx^2$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. We prove that $P_λ$ is a permutation polynomial if and only if either $λ=0$, or $λ\ne0$ and $X^3+X+λ^{-1}$ has no root in $\mathbb{F}_q$. Moreover, the number of admissible parameters is $(q+2)/3$ when $m$ is even and $(q+4)/3$ when $m$ is odd. Thus, admissible parameters exist for every $m\geq2$, and approximately one-third of the elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$ yield permutation polynomials. For every admissible parameter $λ$, we determine the complete Walsh distribution of the balanced Boolean function $f_λ$ parameterized by $P_λ(x+x^2)$ and prove that this distribution is independent of $λ$. For $m\geq3$, these functions have the five-valued Walsh spectrum ${q,0,-q,-2q,-3q}$, while for $m=2$ the spectrum degenerates to four values. As applications, their supports yield projective minimal binary five-weight codes, sets with five hyperplane intersection numbers, and regular cubelike Cayley graphs with six distinct eigenvalues. Finally, for mappings of the form $P(x+x^{-1})$, we construct an infinite family of balanced Boolean functions with simple explicit trace representations.

papers.title: On the Laugesen--Siudeja Conjecture: A Sharp Lower Bound and Failure of the Upper Bound
papers.abstract: We prove the sharp lower bound in the Laugesen--Siudeja conjecture and give a counterexample to its upper bound. For every bounded convex planar domain, the first Dirichlet eigenvalue $λ_1$, the area $A$, and the centroidal polar moment of inertia $I$ satisfy $λ_1A^3/I>9π^2/2$. The constant is approached by thin isosceles triangles. The lower bound follows from a rectangle comparison in the principal directions of the covariance matrix and a planar random-triangle inequality. For the upper bound, we exhibit an isosceles trapezoid on which $λ_1A^3/I>12π^2$, using Temple's inequality and exact arithmetic.

papers.title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
papers.abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

papers.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.

papers.title: Regularizing gravity in the presence of matter fields
papers.abstract: We investigate how matter fields affect spacetime regularity in a class of gravitational theories with second-order field equations in spherical symmetry, of which general relativity is a special case, and which may encode effective corrections from an underlying quantum theory of gravity. Focusing on spherically symmetric black holes and cosmological spacetimes in theories in which vacuum spacetimes display bounded curvature invariants, we derive the conditions under which regular geometries can be supported by static and perturbative scalar fields, electromagnetic fields, and radiation fluids. We discuss the impact of matter on the regularity requirements of curvature boundedness and geodesic completeness relative to vacuum, finding in general that coupling to matter does not eliminate the existence of theories with regular solutions.

papers.title: Linear Convergence of Adaptive Accelerated Gradient Methods: A Unified Framework
papers.abstract: We establish a unified Lyapunov framework for adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives. Conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation ensure eventual linear convergence without assuming stepsize convergence. We verify these conditions for specified AdaNAG-G, smooth unconstrained AC-FGM, and AdaAGM policies and use them to design VC-FG and CC-FG. The verified adaptive main iterations require neither global smoothness nor strong-convexity parameters and avoid restart and backtracking. The framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound. Experiments on four smooth, strongly convex problem families illustrate complementary performance of the new methods.

papers.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
papers.abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.

papers.title: Optimizing MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with burst-mode free-electron laser operation
papers.abstract: Burst-mode X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide a powerful platform for X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments with sub-microsecond temporal resolution, but the achievable performance is constrained in practice by both photon statistics and the sample's dose tolerance. Here, we develop an analytical framework for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of pulsed XPCS measurements, including pulse-to-pulse fluctuations of the incident intensity. We combine this description with dose constraints and show that, for a fixed maximum dose, acquiring fewer frames at higher per-pulse intensity yields a higher SNR than distributing the dose over a larger number of low-intensity frames. The framework is validated against measurements at the European XFEL, where the intensity fluctuations of the investigated operation mode are found to cause only a negligible reduction in SNR. We further introduce and experimentally demonstrate a rolling bunch pattern with three pulses per train and variable pulse spacings. This scheme enables more than an order-of-magnitude increase in the accessible per-pulse intensity while maintaining equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide practical guidelines for optimizing dose-efficient MHz-XPCS experiments and for evaluating future XFEL operation modes.

papers.title: Mass Spectra and Radiative Decay Widths of \(D_{s0}^{*}(2317)^+\), \(D_{s1}(2460)^+\) and \(D'_{s1}(2536)^+\)
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent experimental reports on the radiative decay \(D_{s1}(2460)^{+}\to D_s^{*+}γ\) and the branching-fraction ratio \(\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+}\to D_s^{*+}γ]/\mathcal{B}[D_{s1}(2460)^{+}\to D_s^{+}γ]\), we investigate the mass spectra and radiative decay widths of \(D_{s0}^{*}(2317)^+\), \(D_{s1}(2460)^+\) and \(D_{s1}'(2536)^+\). Within the chiral quark model combined with the Gaussian Expansion Method, the mass spectra obtained agree reasonably well with the experimental data.
