Using data from Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System in South Africa, we examined the spillover effect of household wealth on mortality in the family network. Methods. We analysed cohort data from 2009 to 2018 to estimate the Average Total Effect (ATE) of household wealth on deaths, decomposing this into an Average Direct Effect (ADE) and Average Spillover Effect (ASE). We estimated these quantities separately for all deaths, deaths among children (<5 years old), premature deaths (among ages 15-59), and deaths among elders (60+). Results. Over the study period, 8750 individuals died. Overall, a one standard deviation increase in household wealth led to an ATE of -0.61% (95% CI: -0.74 to -0.48, P<0.001), an ADE of -0.53% (95% CI: -0.63 to -0.42, P<0.001) and an ASE of -0.08% (95% CI: -0.18 to 0.01, P=0.075). For premature mortality, these effect estimates were -0.37% (95% CI: -0.47 to -0.26, P<0.001), -0.29% (95% CI: -0.37 to -0.21, P<0.001), and -0.08% (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.00, P=0.038), respectively. Conclusions. Results provide evidence for the protective effect of household wealth on premature mortality across family relationships.

papers.title: MoRE: Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Physics Robotic World Models
papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.

papers.title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: https://github.com/opatil31/SEANA

papers.title: A Nonadaptive Sparse Fourier Transform in Every Dimension
papers.abstract: Let $G=(\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^d$, of order $N=2^{ad}$. Given point-query access to any complex signal $X$ with Fourier transform $\hat{X}$ over $G$, we provide a randomized algorithm that constructs a $k$-sparse estimate $\widetilde{X}$ via non-adaptive queries such that, with large probability, $\|\widetilde{X}-\hat{X}\|_2^2 \leq C \cdot \|H_k(\hat{X})-\hat{X}\|_2^2$, for an absolute constant $C>0$, where $H_k(\cdot)$ denotes the best $k$-sparse approximation. The constant $C$ can be improved to any desired $1+\varepsilon$ by either supplying a constant-factor estimate on the $k$-sparse tail norm or allowing an arbitrarily small additive error term $δ\|\hat{X}\|_2^2$ on the right-hand side. With a supplied tail estimate, we can also satisfy an $\ell_\infty/\ell_2$ heavy hitters guarantee. For fixed $δ$, the number of samples is $O((k/\varepsilon^2)(\log N)\log(k/\varepsilon))$, and the recovery algorithm requires a polynomial in $(k/\varepsilon)\log N$ exact operations. The algorithm naturally extends to $G=(\mathbb{Z}/b^a\mathbb{Z})^d$ for any fixed integer $b>1$.

papers.title: MoGloss: Joint Motion and Pseudo-Gloss Pretraining for American Sign Language Understanding
papers.abstract: Sign language translation and recognition have been shown to benefit from various pretraining approaches. We propose a novel two-stage pretraining approach for the motion encoder, which first learns to reconstruct masked motion, followed by joint masked prediction of pseudo-gloss units and motion. Pseudo-glosses serve as an intermediate structured representation of natural language text and are obtained from the captions by a large language model. We curate a corpus of about 1,100 hours of American Sign Language from five public datasets, estimate 2D pose for all clips and define an evaluation protocol. We then reproduce state-of-the-art translation methods and evaluate them using the same train and test splits. We propose a translation model built on our pretraining strategy, and this model outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods Uni-Sign and SHuBERT, as well as the YouTube-ASL baseline, on the How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki and OpenASL datasets. Furthermore, the gain from the joint pretraining using motion and pseudo-gloss grows as translation data shrinks. A classifier built on the same encoder also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen isolated sign recognition and outperforms our reproduction of Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.

papers.title: Circuit model for gate-induced excitation of quantum Hall edges tuned by DC gate bias
papers.abstract: Edge excitations, which propagate along the edge of a quantum Hall system, are of great interest in the study of low-dimensional electron systems and mesoscopic transport phenomena. In this study, we investigate the relationship between the input voltage and the excitation waveform for gate-induced excitations. By varying the offset voltage applied to the gate, we observe that the excitation waveform changes from a first-derivative-like response to a response proportional to the input waveform in the time domain. In the frequency domain, we observe that the frequency dependence of the gate excitation changes significantly as the offset voltage crosses the pinch-off voltage. We show that these changes can be described by a single equivalent circuit model with different effective gate-2DEG capacitances on either side of the pinch-off voltage. In addition, we confirm that the effective capacitance obtained from the fitting of the model with the experimental data is consistent with the capacitance calculated from the device structure.

papers.title: The Semi--Fibonacci Partition Tree
papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce a binary tree in which every semi-Fibonacci partition appears exactly once. The left--right address of a vertex gives an explicit formula for the parts of the corresponding partition and encodes statistics such as the largest $2$-adic valuation among its parts. We construct a sign-reversing involution that refines Andrews's parity theorem by determining the difference between the numbers of partitions of a given integer at even and odd depths. Inspired by properties of the Calkin--Wilf tree, we study several parameters of our tree and use them to obtain new results on semi-Fibonacci partitions. We also derive generating functions for partition statistics and determine the average and extremal partition sizes at each level.

papers.title: Counting Elements and Conjugacy Classes of Fixed Genus in Hyperbolic Groups
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a non-elementary hyperbolic group equipped with a word metric. A group element in $G$ has orientable genus $n$ if it can be written as the product of $n$ commutators and no fewer. Similarly, a group element in $G$ has non-orientable genus $m$ if it can be written as the product of $m$ squares and no fewer. We obtain the asymptotic order of growth for both the number of group elements and the number of conjugacy classes in $G$, with length at most $L$, and fixed genus (orientable or non-orientable) $n$. For free groups, our methods give precise asymptotics for each of the counts.

papers.title: Gaussian Quasi-Likelihood Estimation for Nonsynchronously Observed Lévy processes
papers.abstract: We study parametric inference for a two-dimensional simple Lévy process observed at high frequency over an expanding time horizon, where the two components are sampled in a possibly non-synchronous manner. Combining Gaussian quasi-likelihood estimation for Lévy SDEs with the non-synchronous quasi-likelihood methodology, we construct a Gaussian-type quasi-likelihood based on the covariance structure of non-synchronous increments, and we prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimators. The convergence rates coincide with those in the synchronous setting, while the asymptotic variance depends essentially on the sampling design and becomes more complicated under non-synchronicity. To handle the different moment structure of pure-jump Lévy processes, we introduce an additional convergence assumption and provide tractable sufficient conditions linked to the observation scheme. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators.

papers.title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
papers.abstract: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

papers.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
papers.abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

papers.title: RE-CAM: Readout-Enhanced Content-Addressable Memory for Quantitative Similarity Search
papers.abstract: Similarity search is essential to many applications but incurs massive data movement when executed on conventional architectures. Content-addressable memory (CAM) is a promising hardware substrate, as it allows similarity search directly in the CAM array, minimizing data movement and offering both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, conventional CAM array readout produces only binary match results, discarding quantitative similarity information that could be further exploited. Extracting this information requires interpreting the CAM array output voltage that evolves during a CAM search, making the sensing timestamp a crucial design variable alongside the reference voltage and decoding parameter. In this work, we propose RE-CAM, a readout enhancement framework for CAM that is agnostic to memory technology and application, enabling CAM array readout to approximate linear and nonlinear functions with one CAM search. By reusing the comparators to sense the time-varying output voltage multiple times, jointly optimizing the three design variables under system constraints and hardware nonidealities, and co-designing the optimization algorithm and reconfigurable hardware, RE-CAM achieves accurate approximation with low energy and area overhead without introducing a readout throughput bottleneck. Across linear, piecewise-linear, sigmoid, and exponential functions, RE-CAM reduces normalized root mean square error by 10.89% to 24.34% for general approximation and 29.43% to 46.73% when exploiting dataset distribution, compared to a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline with the same comparison budget. Relative to the same baseline, RE-CAM also achieves $8\times$ higher search throughput while reducing energy per search and area by 47% and 39%, respectively.

papers.title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
papers.abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

papers.title: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Gate-level netlists circulate among IP integrators and foundries and can be extracted from chips. Reverse engineering them into readable register-transfer-level (RTL) code would help an adversary understand and modify a design, but remains difficult because word-level operations are scattered across many gates. Large language models (LLMs) can write and optimize RTL, but often fail to recover it from a whole netlist. We propose LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), an LLM-based attack that divides an anonymized netlist into logic cones, has parallel agents rewrite them, and assembles compact RTL. Each cone contains the complete next-state logic of a group of related registers, giving an agent a small, meaningful task. Of five partitioning methods tested, only grouped cones lead to recovery. LOCA keeps only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist and measures its quality by compression. Function-preserving obfuscation does not stop LOCA on the tested designs, whereas unknown keys or hidden cell functions prevent it from proving recovery of the original design. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting. Per-run recovery across models rises from 5% to 74%, at a median cost below one dollar with a low-cost model.

papers.title: Generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states in a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model implemented with Josephson junctions
papers.abstract: We investigate the generation of coherent-state Schrödinger cat states using a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) implemented in a Josephson-junction quantum circuit. We consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation and estimate the resulting two-photon coupling constant. We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with $1/f$ fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit $T_{1}$ decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the $l$-photon JCM ($l=1,2,3,4$), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.

papers.title: Symmetry-resolved spectroscopy of truncation-induced perturbations in loop tensor network renormalization of the six-vertex model
papers.abstract: Tensor network renormalization at finite bond dimension $χ$ introduces truncation errors that are amplified by the renormalization-group (RG) flow. For loop tensor network renormalization (LoopTNR) on the $c=1$ critical line of the six-vertex model, with Luttinger parameter $K$, we identify these errors operator by operator from symmetry-resolved transfer-matrix spectra and conformal perturbation theory. With $O(2)$ symmetry imposed, the dominant error is the dimerization operator, which is allowed because LoopTNR breaks one-site translation. With less symmetry it is the $U(1)$ current or a charge-two vertex operator. The growth of the dimerization per RG step and a parameter-free ratio of its amplitudes agree with conformal perturbation theory to within a few percent. The parameter $K$ drifts slowly, owing to a weak marginal error and to the running induced by the dimerization. A larger $χ$ lowers the initial amplitude of the error for $0.75\le K\le 1.5$ but changes neither the operator nor its growth rate.

papers.title: Learning Spin Hamiltonians from Interacting Magnon Spectra
papers.abstract: A neural network that learns an inverse map inherits the approximations of the forward solver used to generate its training data. We demonstrate this in the inference of spin Hamiltonians from synthetic neutron-scattering spectra and show how a fast many-body solver can overcome the limitation of linear spin-wave theory (LSWT). We consider a family of anisotropic triangular-lattice spin Hamiltonians at fields just above saturation, where magnon interactions shift and broaden the spectrum in ways that LSWT cannot capture. Using the truncated Hilbert-space ladder (THL) method, we compute the dynamical spin structure factor (DSSF) nonperturbatively within the one- and two-magnon space. THL is fast enough to generate large training sets of DSSF spectra, enabling us to train neural networks that accurately predict Hamiltonian parameters. By empirically benchmarking several neural-network architectures, we find that a one-dimensional convolutional network performs best. A learned forward decoder then reconstructs the DSSF from the predicted parameters, providing a rapid self-consistency check and a visualization of the predicted response. When interactions are strong, networks trained on LSWT and THL spectra infer markedly different parameters. Analysis of the Fisher information matrix shows that the measurement protocol, including which spin-correlation components are resolved and the momentum cut, determines which couplings can be identified. Combining machine learning with fast many- body theory is therefore essential for quantitative Hamiltonian inference from scattering data.

papers.title: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation
papers.abstract: Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. In a task with several phases, this budget must be divided among the phases, and the phase in which the base policy fails is not necessarily the phase in which a correction most improves task completion. We formalize this distinction through the completion gain: the change in full-task completion probability when, during a single phase, a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy's action. We decompose the completion gain into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase, and we estimate it from paired episodes. The positive estimates determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases. In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, whereas the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase; gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget. In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release; in a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

papers.title: The Prediction-to-Decision Gap: First-Action Informativity in Data-Driven Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) applies only the first input of an optimized sequence before replanning. Do the available data determine this input? We define first-action informativity as agreement across data-compatible models at a fixed history and reference, with common MPC settings. For autoregressive models with exogenous inputs (ARX) and unconstrained quadratic MPC, we show that first-action agreement and prediction agreement under a fixed input sequence do not imply one another. We give structural conditions for action agreement without requiring unique model identification. When actions disagree, we quantify their mean-squared deviation from the fitted model's input under a specific parameter distribution. We approximate this measure using local sensitivities and parameter covariance. Analytical and numerical examples illustrate how model uncertainty affects predictions and actions differently. The framework evaluates model uncertainty through its effect on the first action MPC is about to apply.

papers.title: Kakutani equivalence of higher rank unipotent abelian actions I
papers.abstract: We study Kakutani equivalence of higher-rank abelian unipotent actions. We construct a Kakutani invariant for general $\mathbb{R}^n$-actions and establish a quantitative vanishing criterion. By this criterion, we prove that ergodic abelian horocyclic actions on finite-volume quotients of connected semisimple Lie groups are loosely Kronecker. We also include a proof of the Abramov entropy formula for time changes of Rn-actions, following the strategy developed by Nadler.

papers.title: Design and Forecasts for a Rubin Twilight Program for Nearby Type Ia Supernovae
papers.abstract: Nearby Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are important for supernova cosmology, but saturation in 30 s exposures, gaps in light-curve sampling, and the footprint of Vera C. Rubin Observatory's baseline Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) survey limit the nearby sample. To improve the low-$z$ sample, we propose a twilight follow-up program using Rubin Observatory for 1-5 s griz exposures at solar altitudes $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -9^\circ$. Using simulations of one year of WFD observations, we find that twilight follow-up adds 230 quality-selected SNe Ia from an external sample drawn primarily from the Transient Name Server (TNS). At $z<0.08$, the usable sample increases from 368 to 643 SNe Ia, including 50 WFD events recovered by refitting their light curves with twilight photometry. Combining these twilight observations with high-redshift WFD and Deep Drilling Field samples increases the statistical-only dark-energy $(w_0,w_a)$ figure of merit from 49.3 to 58.3 (18%) and reduces $σ(w_a)$ by 10%. For measurements of structure growth at $0.02 \le z<0.06$, the fractional uncertainty on $fσ_8$ decreases from 0.783 to 0.305. Restricting the program to $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -11^\circ$ reduces the dark-energy improvement to 7.2%. These short exposures could also provide unsaturated photometry of potential distance-ladder calibrators at $z<0.02$.
authors: the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration

papers.title: Arithmetic Upper and Lower Bounds for the Denumerant Function III
papers.abstract: We extend the denumerant to a weighted denumerant, the sum of a function $μ$ over the solutions in non-negative integers of $a_1x_1+\cdots+a_kx_k=n$. For the monomial weights $x_1^{α_1}\cdots x_k^{α_k}$, with exponents $α_i\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$, we prove upper and lower bounds of the kind of those of the first paper of this series (arXiv:2204.13689), with an explicit constant and explicit shifts. As an example of application, summing these bounds over all the numbers $a_1,\dots,a_k$ we find, by elementary means, the asymptotic main term of the sums $\sum_{y_1+\cdots+y_k=n}σ_{α_1}(y_1)\cdotsσ_{α_k}(y_k)$ of products of divisor functions, for every $k$ and for real exponents $α_i\neq0$ of either sign.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.

papers.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

papers.title: Variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups
papers.abstract: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when $G$ is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on $T^*(\mathbb R\times G)$ whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on $SO(3)^N$ with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on $SO(3)$ illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.

papers.title: First $Ω_{\rm m}-w$ Measurement Using Only Fast Radio Burst Observations
papers.abstract: Though fast radio bursts (FRBs) are widely advocated as a dark energy probe, no valid $Ω_m-w$ constraint has been obtained exclusively from FRB data to date. Benefiting from a rapidly growing localized sample and a novel statistical framework for modeling the dispersion measure (DM), we report the first simultaneous inference of the matter density $Ω_m$ and dark energy equation of state parameter $w$ from FRBs alone, without external observational priors on these two parameters. We combine a multi-parameter emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum with a physically motivated electron prescription to construct a cosmology-dependent cosmic-DM distribution. Within this unified analysis framework, the mean and variance of DM respond self-consistently to the same underlying cosmology, directly connecting the FRB likelihood to both cosmic expansion and structure growth. Analyzing 125 localized FRBs at $0.105\leq z\leq2.148$, we obtain $Ω_m = 0.33^{+0.10}_{-0.11}$ and $w = -0.80^{+0.28}_{-0.38}$ under the flat $w$CDM model. We find a new positive $Ω_m-w$ degeneracy in the FRB posterior, opposite to the strong anticorrelation derived from Type Ia supernovae, offering a complementary test of dark energy properties and highlighting their potential in future precision cosmological studies.

papers.title: Prescribed Bayesian Efficiency under Lifetime Adjustment Costs
papers.abstract: A Bayesian learner may retain an issued action while updating its posterior, trading predictive loss against adjustment charges. We assume population curvature, boundary control, an order-$1/n$ lower bound on expected posterior uncertainty about the optimal action, and an observable unbiased gradient witness whose squared norms are uniformly integrable. Sample losses may be unbounded or nonconvex. Cumulative expected excess measures the loss increase relative to current predictive Bayes actions. For bounded nonnegative nondecreasing charges $c$ with $c(0)=0$ and nondecreasing profiles $G: \mathbb{N} \to [1,\infty)$ with $G(J)=o(J)$, we characterize joint attainability of cumulative expected excess $O(G(J))$ at horizons $T=2^J$ and finite expected lifetime charge. Here $J$ indexes logarithmic time. The criterion is finiteness of a prefix-constrained allocation of tracking-error allowances across action-distance scales, equivalently its decreasing-weight dual. Adaptive timing and private randomization do not enlarge the attainable region. For each feasible pair, a horizon-independent deterministic checkpoint policy attains the profile with lifetime-cost moments of every positive order. For excess $O((\log T)^r)$, $0<r<1$, every policy needs $Ω((\log T)^{2-r})$ revisions in expectation, and a charge-independent schedule achieves a matching pathwise upper bound for every feasible charge. We verify the assumptions for logistic decision models with nondegenerate covariates, finite second moments and a locally positive smooth prior density, including fixed-ridge models with unbounded parameter priors.

papers.title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.

papers.title: Painlevé transcendents in the defocusing Hirota equation with non-zero boundary conditions
papers.abstract: We consider the Cauchy problem for the defocusing Hirota equation with non-zero boundary conditions \begin{align*} &iq_t+ q_{xx}-2\left(|q|^2-1\right)q +i\left(q_{xxx}-6|q|^2q_x\right)=0,\\ &q(x,0)=q_0(x)\to\pm 1, \quad x\to\pm\infty, \end{align*} which can be characterized using a Riemann-Hilbert problem through the inverse scattering transform. With the $\bar{\partial}$-steepest descent method and double scaling limit technique, we derive the long-time asymptotics of the solution in two transition regions \begin{align*} \mathcal{P}_{a} :=\left\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{+}: \left| {x}/{t}-a\right|t^{2/3}<C\right\}, \quad a\in\{-4,-8\}, \end{align*} where $C>0$ is a constant. It is shown that the asymptotic expansions in two transition regions can be expressed in terms of the Hastings--McLeod solution of the Painlevé II equation in the generic case and Ablowitz--Segur solutions in the non-generic case.

papers.title: Data-driven Linearization of Operational Dynamics of Soft Open Points in Power Distribution Networks
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel data-driven linearization of operational power losses in a Soft Open Point (SOP). The proposed learning-based representation, combined with the standard segmentation of the quadratic device capacity inequalities, linearizes the operational dynamics of SOPs in unbalanced power distribution network applications without a significant drop in power loss estimation accuracy. The technique was tested in three applications using a three-phase extension of the IEEE 33-bus network. The case studies include a sizing application for a multi-terminal phase-changing soft open point (PCSOP), an operational optimization application for an active distribution network featuring a PCSOP, and a system simulation engine built for a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) application that trains an agent to optimally dispatch a PCSOP in an unbalanced distribution network. The results of the three case studies were validated against the standard nonlinear AC load-flow representations and point to the efficacy of the proposed solution.

papers.title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage
papers.abstract: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $α_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10α_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21α_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $α_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $α_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$α_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.

papers.title: Subexponential Algorithms for Continuous Euclidean $k$-Means in Subpolylogarithmic Dimension
papers.abstract: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{Q}^d$ and an integer $k$, the continuous Euclidean $k$-means problem asks for $k$ centers in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that minimize the sum of squared distances from the input points to their nearest centers. In one dimension, the problem can be solved in polynomial time by dynamic programming. In higher dimensions, the algorithm of Inaba, Katoh, and Imai [SoCG 1994] runs in polynomial time when both $k$ and $d$ are fixed. Mahajan, Nimbhorkar, and Varadarajan [TCS 2012] showed that the problem is NP-hard even in the plane when $k$ is part of the input, answering a question of Dasgupta [2008]. In this paper, we give a deterministic exact algorithm for continuous Euclidean $k$-means. For arbitrary $k$ and $d=(\log n)^{o(1)}$, the algorithm runs in $O^*(2^{o(n)})$ time and uses polynomial space. Aman, Karthik C. S., and Punna [ESA 2024] asked whether the $2^n$ time bound for Euclidean $k$-means can be improved in high dimensions. Our result gives an affirmative answer to the corresponding question in subpolylogarithmic dimension.

papers.title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1): The MERge processing
papers.abstract: The ESA satellite mission \Euclid was launched in July 2023 and started its regular observing mode in February 2024. The data from the \Euclid instruments Visible Camera (VIS) and the Near IR Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) are complemented by ground-based imaging data in the $u$, $g$ $r$, $i$, and $z$ bands to enable the determination of photometric redshifts and other galaxy properties. This paper describes the MERge processing function (MER PF) that has been developed and run for the Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). The aim of the MER PF is to detect objects in the \Euclid imaging data, measure their properties, and combine them into a single multi-wavelength catalogue. In this paper we illustrate the design of the MER PF and introduce the different photometric methods applied to the data, which are Kron total flux, aperture photometry on Point Spread Functions (PSF) -matched images, template fitting photometry, and Sérsic fitting photometry. We also present the various morphological measurements and quality flags that improve the scientific content of the output catalogues and better characterize the detected sources. We illustrate the processing and measurements that help to validate the MER PF results, which is an essential step to qualify the output for the public DR1 release. We discuss the global assessment of the photometric homogeneity and provide an internal comparison of our processing results. In addition, we give an extensive overview of the DR1 output data and the various processing scenarios

papers.title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
papers.abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $Φ$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.

papers.title: High-precision timing of seven binary millisecond pulsars with the European Pulsar Timing Array
papers.abstract: Binary millisecond pulsars (MSPs) serve as exceptional astrophysical laboratories for a wide range of astrophysical studies, all of which rely on precise property measurements allowed by pulsar timing. In this paper, we present high-precision timing solutions for seven binary MSPs monitored by the European Pulsar Timing Array. By combining data collected from the five largest radio telescopes in Europe as well as through their coherently combined form, the Large European Array for Pulsars, we achieved phase-coherent timing solutions for all seven pulsars. We conducted a Bayesian timing and noise analysis on the combined data, yielding measurements of astrometric and orbital parameters either for the first time or with broadly improved precision. For PSRs J0125-2327, J1741+1351, and J2043+1711, we determined their distances and transverse velocities from astrometric measurements, and we inferred their masses via Shapiro delay measurements. Additionally, we examined the various contributions to the secular orbital-period variations for PSRs J0125-2327, J1125+7819, and J1741+1351, and we estimated their kinematic distances. For PSRs J0125-2327 and J1741+1351, we detected the signature of annual-orbital parallax in the timing data. This allowed us to derive a strongly favoured, unique solution for the orbital ascending node and inclination angle for PSR J0125-2327 and a tightly constrained ascending node for PSR J1741+1351. Moreover, we used the orbital periods and their derivatives for several binary MSPs to place upper limits on gravitational-wave strain in both the sub-nanohertz and microhertz frequency regimes. Our results show that the orbits of binary MSPs could provide stringent constraints in the microhertz range, thereby possibly complementing standard pulsar timing array analyses in the future.

papers.title: Two Principles for Autoregressive Language Modeling
papers.abstract: We investigate the functional differentiation learned by RoPE Transformers to derive principles for autoregressive language modeling. We introduce two intervention-based metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) measures how removing a frequency contribution changes a head's full attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) isolates the effect of rotary modulation. In Qwen3 and Llama3.1, these metrics distinguish retrieval from positional modeling, while individual heads can exhibit both functions. A mid-low-frequency Global Positional Band (GPBand) separates their frequency dependencies and tracks the training sequence length in controlled experiments, suggesting that global positional fitting can hinder zero-shot length extrapolation. These findings motivate two principles. (1) Functional Organization: retrieval and positional functions should be assigned separately and mixed within layers with layer-specific allocation; and (2) Positional Dependence: positional modeling should operate only locally, while global access should rely on position-independent retrieval. Matched pretraining from scratch and targeted architectural ablations at 380M and 1.4B parameters support both principles and highlight the importance of mechanism choice in realizing each function. Together, these findings suggest a promising route toward architectural innovation grounded in the functional requirements of autoregressive language modeling.

papers.title: What Does a Temporal Benchmark Score Measure? Decomposing Channel Use in Video VLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: A score on a temporal video question answering benchmark is meant to measure that a model has temporal understanding, but it conflates two questions. (1) is the question even temporal, does it need several frames and their order? And (2) when it does, does the model recover the order from the pixels, or read it off the positional encoding (RoPE)? Most of a temporal score answers neither, since a single frame and answer priors often carry it, and the field's validity checks, frame-shuffle sensitivity and multi-frame gain, speak only to (1). For (2) we score a reversal conflict, frames reversed while RoPE stays forward, two ways: label-free, as the accuracy lost against the forward labels, and against reversed labels wherever labels transform deterministically under time reversal. This separates a model that follows the reversed content from one merely disrupted. The two readings dissociate two similarly scoring models at both model scales. Qwen3-VL answers the reversed event it actually sees, reading the visual sequence. Molmo2 correctly reports a backwards video when positions agree, and flipping only the RoPE indices flips its prediction to the forward events, i.e. it reads positions. We call these regimes visual-sequence-dominant and position-dominant. Controls show reversed content is processable whenever the channels agree, and that both families share a bias toward describing events as running forward (arrow-of-time prior) that, being similar in strength, cannot by itself account for the dissociation. The distinction matters because the two channels fail on opposite inputs: two models with the same score are not interchangeable.

papers.title: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.
